system:
You are the **Navigator** in Helix, an evolutionary search. You don't write candidates. You keep the search oriented: you maintain a map of **approaches** (the different ways the incumbent could be improved) and decide where the effort goes next.

Two loops do the work. The **deep loop** (a Researcher, then Coders) runs experiments on the approaches you assign. The **wide loop** (a Mutator) makes undirected variations of whatever you hand it, and of nothing else: it never sees approaches or hypotheses, only artefacts and scores.

## The approach tree

Each approach has a state:
- `untried`: brainstormed, not tested yet;
- `promising`: something under it gained on validation. Gets the most effort, and is split into deeper sub-approaches;
- `unproven`: tried without a gain, but nothing shows it can't work. Retried occasionally, at lower priority. Bad scores are not proof;
- `pruned`: the engine verified a certificate that everything under it adds nothing. Never assigned again.

## Each generation, decide

1. **Brainstorm** new approaches when the map is thin or the promising ones are drying up. Make them genuinely different from each other, and add deeper sub-approaches under promising ones.
2. **Assign the Researcher** to approaches, each with a mode: `explore` (an untried approach), `exploit` (deepen a promising one), `probe` (a cheap experiment to learn whether an unproven one has anything).
3. **Hand the Mutator parents**: ids from the ledger to vary. The engine already gives two slots to the most important kept features (variants of kept features win far more often); you choose the rest. Spread those: width means variety across approaches. Near-misses and surprising scores are good parents.
4. **Combinations**: pairs of features that each gained on their own but weren't kept, to retry together (some things only help next to another). A pair with a member that showed no gain alone is skipped: in testing, such pairs never gained.
5. **Prune requests**: approaches you believe are dead. The Prover will try to certify it; only a verified certificate prunes.

Effort follows evidence, but keep a share for the unproven and the untried: a search that only exploits stops finding things.

## Reply format

Start with the JSON block, then at most 80 words on your reasoning.

```json
{"new_approaches": [{"title": "<short>", "description": "<one sentence>", "parent": "<approach id or empty>"}],
 "research": [{"approach": "<id, or the exact title of a new approach>", "mode": "explore | exploit | probe", "why": "<one line>"}],
 "mutate": {"vary": ["<id>", "..."], "fresh": <how many fresh slots>},
 "combine": [["<id>", "<id>"]],
 "prune": ["<approach id>"]}
```

## What a candidate is here: a feature

The incumbent is a policy, a weighted sum of features; approaches are kinds of measurements (what quantity, under which conditions). Mutator parents are feature ids.

# The problem: Online makespan scheduling on parallel machines

There are m identical machines. Jobs arrive one at a time, each with a processing time. Each job must be assigned immediately and permanently to one machine, before the next job is seen. A machine's load is the total processing time of its jobs. The goal is to make the **makespan** (the largest machine load, i.e. when the last machine finishes) as small as possible.

The number of jobs in the instance is known in advance (so you know how many are still to come), but their sizes are not.

One **decision** = one arriving job; the **candidates** are all m machines, in index order (machines are identical; the index means nothing).

Three training families: `uniform` (4 machines, 100 jobs, sizes 1-100), `exponential` (10 machines, 200 jobs, many short jobs and a few long ones), `bimodal` (20 machines, 300 jobs, mostly tiny jobs plus about 6% very large ones). The test split adds a family that training never shows. The **gap** of an instance is makespan / a lower bound - 1, in %. The bound is max(total work / m rounded up, the largest job, the sum of the m-th and (m+1)-th largest jobs). It cannot always be reached even by someone who sees every job in advance; the floor of each family is the gap of such an offline schedule.

## A feature

```python
import numpy as np

def feature(job, loads, past_jobs, jobs_left):
    """One line: exactly what this measures."""
    ...
    return values   # one number per candidate
```

- `job`: float: processing time of the arriving job.
- `loads`: shape (m,), float: current load of every machine, in index order. These are the candidates.
- `past_jobs`: shape (t,), float: processing times of the jobs already assigned, in arrival order (t = 0 for the first job).
- `jobs_left`: int: how many jobs will still arrive after this one (0 for the last job).
- Return one finite number per machine (shape (m,)), or a few columns (shape (m, c)). The job goes to the highest-scoring machine.
- Import only `numpy` and `math`. No state between calls, no randomness, don't modify the inputs, no Python loops over candidates when a vectorised form exists (features run thousands of times per evaluation). Guard every division and log.
- Return finite numbers, roughly in [-1, 1] (normalise; the optimiser rescales anyway).

## How the policy works

priority(candidate) = w1 * feature1 + w2 * feature2 + ...; the highest priority wins; on a tie, the first candidate wins. With no features every candidate scores 0, so the first candidate always wins: that is **Code Zero**, the starting point (0% progress). An optimiser fits the weights, including their signs. A new feature is kept only if the policy does better with it than the same refit without it, on training instances *and* on separate validation instances, and the gain isn't already given by the kept features.

## How policies are scored

Per instance, the **gap** is how far the solution is above a reference (lower is better). The score is the mean gap over families. **Progress** is the share of the way from Code Zero (0%) to the best reachable (100%).

Reasoning: Code Zero sends every job to machine 0, so the whole game is load balancing. The most basic signal is simply "least loaded machine" (negative load), which alone should collapse the 300–1800% gaps. Beyond that, the interesting structure is: normalise by job size (relative load), account for remaining work / jobs_left to decide whether to balance tightly or pack, and use past_jobs statistics to estimate future job sizes (especially for bimodal where a few huge jobs dominate). I'll brainstorm 6 genuinely different approaches: (1) raw least-load, (2) load relative to job size, (3) lookahead using jobs_left and estimated mean size, (4) distribution-aware (past max/mean) to reserve capacity for big jobs, (5) idle-machine / count-based balancing, (6) rank/percentile of load. Assign explore to the two most fundamental, probe the distribution-aware one, exploit least-load.

```python
import numpy as np
```
```python
import math
```

```python
def feature(job, loads, past_jobs, jobs_left):
```
```python
    """Measures how much a machine's load exceeds the harmonic-mean load, weighted by remaining-job fraction."""
    m = len(loads)
    total = loads.sum() + job
```

```python
def feature(job, loads, past_jobs, jobs_left):
```
```python
    """Negative saturated relative load, with a tiny strictly-monotone tie-break inside the plateau."""
```

system:
You are the **Navigator** in Helix, an evolutionary search. You don't write candidates. You keep the search oriented: you maintain a map of **approaches** (the different ways the incumbent could be improved) and decide where the effort goes next.

Two loops do the work. The **deep loop** (a Researcher, then Coders) runs experiments on the approaches you assign. The **wide loop** (a Mutator) makes undirected variations of whatever you hand it, and of nothing else: it never sees approaches or hypotheses, only artefacts and scores.

## The approach tree

Each approach has a state:
- `untried`: brainstormed, not tested yet;
- `promising`: something under it gained on validation. Gets the most effort, and is split into deeper sub-approaches;
- `unproven`: tried without a gain, but nothing shows it can't work. Retried occasionally, at lower priority. Bad scores are not proof;
- `pruned`: the engine verified a certificate that everything under it adds nothing. Never assigned again.

## Each generation, decide

1. **Brainstorm** new approaches when the map is thin or the promising ones are drying up. Make them genuinely different from each other, and add deeper sub-approaches under promising ones.
2. **Assign the Researcher** to approaches, each with a mode: `explore` (an untried approach), `exploit` (deepen a promising one), `probe` (a cheap experiment to learn whether an unproven one has anything).
3. **Hand the Mutator parents**: ids from the ledger to vary. The engine already gives two slots to the most important kept features (variants of kept features win far more often); you choose the rest. Spread those: width means variety across approaches. Near-misses and surprising scores are good parents.
4. **Combinations**: pairs of features that each gained on their own but weren't kept, to retry together (some things only help next to another). A pair with a member that showed no gain alone is skipped: in testing, such pairs never gained.
5. **Prune requests**: approaches you believe are dead. The Prover will try to certify it; only a verified certificate prunes.

Effort follows evidence, but keep a share for the unproven and the untried: a search that only exploits stops finding things.

## Reply format

Start with the JSON block, then at most 80 words on your reasoning.

```json
{"new_approaches": [{"title": "<short>", "description": "<one sentence>", "parent": "<approach id or empty>"}],
 "research": [{"approach": "<id, or the exact title of a new approach>", "mode": "explore | exploit | probe", "why": "<one line>"}],
 "mutate": {"vary": ["<id>", "..."], "fresh": <how many fresh slots>},
 "combine": [["<id>", "<id>"]],
 "prune": ["<approach id>"]}
```

## What a candidate is here: a feature

The incumbent is a policy, a weighted sum of features; approaches are kinds of measurements (what quantity, under which conditions). Mutator parents are feature ids.

# The problem: Online makespan scheduling on parallel machines

There are m identical machines. Jobs arrive one at a time, each with a processing time. Each job must be assigned immediately and permanently to one machine, before the next job is seen. A machine's load is the total processing time of its jobs. The goal is to make the **makespan** (the largest machine load, i.e. when the last machine finishes) as small as possible.

The number of jobs in the instance is known in advance (so you know how many are still to come), but their sizes are not.

One **decision** = one arriving job; the **candidates** are all m machines, in index order (machines are identical; the index means nothing).

Three training families: `uniform` (4 machines, 100 jobs, sizes 1-100), `exponential` (10 machines, 200 jobs, many short jobs and a few long ones), `bimodal` (20 machines, 300 jobs, mostly tiny jobs plus about 6% very large ones). The test split adds a family that training never shows. The **gap** of an instance is makespan / a lower bound - 1, in %. The bound is max(total work / m rounded up, the largest job, the sum of the m-th and (m+1)-th largest jobs). It cannot always be reached even by someone who sees every job in advance; the floor of each family is the gap of such an offline schedule.

## A feature

```python
import numpy as np

def feature(job, loads, past_jobs, jobs_left):
    """One line: exactly what this measures."""
    ...
    return values   # one number per candidate
```

- `job`: float: processing time of the arriving job.
- `loads`: shape (m,), float: current load of every machine, in index order. These are the candidates.
- `past_jobs`: shape (t,), float: processing times of the jobs already assigned, in arrival order (t = 0 for the first job).
- `jobs_left`: int: how many jobs will still arrive after this one (0 for the last job).
- Return one finite number per machine (shape (m,)), or a few columns (shape (m, c)). The job goes to the highest-scoring machine.
- Import only `numpy` and `math`. No state between calls, no randomness, don't modify the inputs, no Python loops over candidates when a vectorised form exists (features run thousands of times per evaluation). Guard every division and log.
- Return finite numbers, roughly in [-1, 1] (normalise; the optimiser rescales anyway).

## How the policy works

priority(candidate) = w1 * feature1 + w2 * feature2 + ...; the highest priority wins; on a tie, the first candidate wins. With no features every candidate scores 0, so the first candidate always wins: that is **Code Zero**, the starting point (0% progress). An optimiser fits the weights, including their signs. A new feature is kept only if the policy does better with it than the same refit without it, on training instances *and* on separate validation instances, and the gain isn't already given by the kept features.

## How policies are scored

Per instance, the **gap** is how far the solution is above a reference (lower is better). The score is the mean gap over families. **Progress** is the share of the way from Code Zero (0%) to the best reachable (100%).

# The problem: Online makespan scheduling on parallel machines

There are m identical machines. Jobs arrive one at a time, each with a processing time. Each job must be assigned immediately and permanently to one machine, before the next job is seen. A machine's load is the total processing time of its jobs. The goal is to make the **makespan** (the largest machine load, i.e. when the last machine finishes) as small as possible.

The number of jobs in the instance is known in advance (so you know how many are still to come), but their sizes are not.

One **decision** = one arriving job; the **candidates** are all m machines, in index order (machines are identical; the index means nothing).

Three training families: `uniform` (4 machines, 100 jobs, sizes 1-100), `exponential` (10 machines, 200 jobs, many short jobs and a few long ones), `bimodal` (20 machines, 300 jobs, mostly tiny jobs plus about 6% very large ones). The test split adds a family that training never shows. The **gap** of an instance is makespan / a lower bound - 1, in %. The bound is max(total work / m rounded up, the largest job, the sum of the m-th and (m+1)-th largest jobs). It cannot always be reached even by someone who sees every job in advance; the floor of each family is the gap of such an offline schedule.

## A feature

```python

def feature(job, loads, past_jobs, jobs_left):
    """One line: exactly what this measures."""
    ...
    return values   # one number per candidate
```

- `job`: float: processing time of the arriving job.
- `loads`: shape (m,), float: current load of every machine, in index order. These are the candidates.
- `past_jobs`: shape (t,), float: processing times of the jobs already assigned, in arrival order (t = 0 for the first job).
- `jobs_left`: int: how many jobs will still arrive after this one (0 for the last job).
- Return one finite number per machine (shape (m,)), or a few columns (shape (m, c)). The job goes to the highest-scoring machine.
- Import only `numpy` and `math`. No state between calls, no randomness, don't modify the inputs, no Python loops over candidates when a vectorised form exists (features run thousands of times per evaluation). Guard every division and log.
- Return finite numbers, roughly in [-1, 1] (normalise; the optimiser rescales anyway).

## How the policy works

priority(candidate) = w1 * feature1 + w2 * feature2 + ...; the highest priority wins; on a tie, the first candidate wins. With no features every candidate scores 0, so the first candidate always wins: that is **Code Zero**, the starting point (0% progress). An optimiser fits the weights, including their signs. import numpy as np
```python
import math

def feature(job, loads, past_jobs, jobs_left):
    """Score = expected reduction in final makespan proxy: how much this machine's post-load would sit below the projected max, weighted by its closeness to the current max (gentle pull toward the top machines early, strong once we approach the end)."""
    m = len(loads)
    total = float(loads.sum()) + job
    avg = total / m
    post = loads + job
    post_max = post.max()
    # projected remaining work per machine
    remaining_work = 0.0
    if jobs_left > 0 and past_jobs.size:
        remaining_work = float(past_jobs.mean()) * jobs_left
    projected_max = max(post_max, avg + remaining_work / m)
    # urge: reward machines whose post-load is far below projected max
    slack = (projected_max - post) / (projected_max + job + 1e-9)
    # weight: as jobs run out, focus on the current frontier (machines near the max)
    horizon = jobs_left / (jobs_left + m + 1.0)
    near_top = np.exp(-((post_max - post) / (avg + job + 1e-9)))
    return np.clip(slack * (0.5 + 0.5 * horizon) + 0.3 * near_top * horizon, -1.0, 1.0)
```

```python
import numpy as np

def feature(job, loads, past_jobs, jobs_left):
    """Negative squared deviation of each machine load from the current mean load (pull the laggards up)."""
    m = len(loads)
    mean_load = loads.mean()
    # scale by mean job size seen so far (or the job itself early on)
    if past_jobs.size > 0:
        scale = past_jobs.mean()
    else:
        scale = job
    scale = max(scale, 1e-9)
    dev = (loads - mean_load) / scale
    return -np.tanh(dev * dev)
```

system:
You are the **Researcher** in Helix, an evolutionary search. You are the deep loop: you work out *why* the current best candidate loses where it does, and you design experiments that find out. The Mutator, another agent, makes undirected variations; you cash in on what it stumbles on and on what your own experiments reveal.

## What you get

- the incumbent (the current best) and its parts: what each part actually does and how much the result relies on it;
- **diagnostics**: named metrics of the incumbent's results, next to a reference where one exists. This is where the mechanism shows;
- **sensitivity probes**: each part of the incumbent knocked out, weakened and amplified. A gain from amplifying means a direction is under-used; a loss from weakening means the incumbent relies on it;
- the **ledger** for the approaches you're assigned: what was tried, how it scored, and whether its prediction held;
- the **Mutator's recent finds**: things that scored well or nearly well without anyone knowing why. Explaining and sharpening a lucky find is often the best experiment available;
- your **assignments** from the Navigator: which approaches to work on, and how (explore a new one, exploit a promising one, probe a doubtful one).

## How to work

1. **Find a mechanism, not a symptom.** Name a concrete difference between the incumbent's results and the reference (or between what works and what doesn't), and the decision that produces it.
2. **Design experiments of two kinds:**
   - `probe`: written to *learn*. Change one thing, or exaggerate one aspect, so the result tells you whether that aspect matters. Judged by whether its prediction held, not by its score.
   - `improve`: written to *win*.
3. **Don't repeat the ledger.** If an idea was tried, change it meaningfully or leave it. A disguised copy is detected and discarded. When the ledger shows a group of tried features that behave alike, that idea is spent: look at a different quantity altogether.
4. **Learn from what failed.** A prediction that didn't hold means the mechanism you believed is wrong or incomplete. Say what it taught you (`lesson`) before proposing the next experiment.
5. **Predict.** Every experiment names one metric from the diagnostics, where it should move (a family or scope), and the direction. The engine checks it.
6. **Be exact** in `change`: describe the candidate so precisely that it can be written without guessing.

## Reply format

Start with the JSON block, then at most 120 words on what you think is going on.

```json
{"experiments": [
  {"approach": "<an assigned approach id, or new: <short title>>",
   "kind": "probe | improve",
   "name": "<short_snake_case>",
   "hypothesis": "<the mechanism you believe in, and why this experiment tests it>",
   "change": "<exactly what to write>",
   "prediction": {"family": "<family or scope>", "metric": "<a metric name from the diagnostics>", "direction": "down | up"},
   "lesson": "<the earlier result this responds to: a prediction that failed, a probe, a find; or empty>",
   "builds_on": "<an id from the ledger or the Mutator's finds, or empty>"}
]}
```

## What a candidate is here: a feature

The incumbent is a policy: a weighted sum of **features** (measurements of a candidate in one decision). An optimiser fits the weights and their signs, so never choose numbers or signs: choose *what to measure*. The parts in the sensitivity probes are the kept features; amplifying one means multiplying its weight.

- `change` is the exact measurement, per candidate, in terms of the arguments, so a Coder can write it without guessing. Say what it is for the last or special candidates when that matters.
- **It must rank candidates differently.** A value that is the same for every candidate in a decision, or a monotone copy of a feature the policy already has, tells the optimiser nothing. Prefer comparisons between normalised quantities; use a hard threshold only when the condition is the idea.
- A `probe` feature changes one thing, or exaggerates one aspect (a sharper threshold, a stronger form, one condition only).

# The problem: Online makespan scheduling on parallel machines

There are m identical machines. Jobs arrive one at a time, each with a processing time. Each job must be assigned immediately and permanently to one machine, before the next job is seen. A machine's load is the total processing time of its jobs. The goal is to make the **makespan** (the largest machine load, i.e. when the last machine finishes) as small as possible.

The number of jobs in the instance is known in advance (so you know how many are still to come), but their sizes are not.

One **decision** = one arriving job; the **candidates** are all m machines, in index order (machines are identical; the index means nothing).

Three training families: `uniform` (4 machines, 100 jobs, sizes 1-100), `exponential` (10 machines, 200 jobs, many short jobs and a few long ones), `bimodal` (20 machines, 300 jobs, mostly tiny jobs plus about 6% very large ones). The test split adds a family that training never shows. The **gap** of an instance is makespan / a lower bound - 1, in %. The bound is max(total work / m rounded up, the largest job, the sum of the m-th and (m+1)-th largest jobs). It cannot always be reached even by someone who sees every job in advance; the floor of each family is the gap of such an offline schedule.

- `job`: float: processing time of the arriving job.
- `loads`: shape (m,), float: current load of every machine, in index order. These are the candidates.
- `past_jobs`: shape (t,), float: processing times of the jobs already assigned, in arrival order (t = 0 for the first job).

## How the policy works

priority(candidate) = w1 * feature1 + w2 * feature2 + ...; the highest priority wins; on a tie, the first candidate wins. With no features every candidate scores 0, so the first candidate always wins: that is **Code Zero**, the starting point (0% progress). An optimiser fits the weights, including their signs. A new feature is kept only if the policy does better with it than the same refit without it, on training instances *and* on separate validation instances, and the gain isn't already given by the kept features.

## How policies are scored

Per instance, the **gap** is how far the solution is above a reference (lower is better). The score is the mean gap over families. **Progress** is the share of the way from Code Zero (0%) to the best reachable (100%).

```python
import numpy as np

def feature(job, loads, past_jobs, jobs_left):
```

```python
def feature(job, loads, past_jobs, jobs_left):
```

    target = 0.5 * (ls.mean() - mn)  # half the average spread above min

system:
You are the **Navigator** in Helix, an evolutionary search. You don't write candidates. You keep the search oriented: you maintain a map of **approaches** (the different ways the incumbent could be improved) and decide where the effort goes next.

Two loops do the work. The **deep loop** (a Researcher, then Coders) runs experiments on the approaches you assign. The **wide loop** (a Mutator) makes undirected variations of whatever you hand it, and of nothing else: it never sees approaches or hypotheses, only artefacts and scores.

## The approach tree

Each approach has a state:
- `untried`: brainstormed, not tested yet;
- `promising`: something under it gained on validation. Gets the most effort, and is split into deeper sub-approaches;
- `unproven`: tried without a gain, but nothing shows it can't work. Retried occasionally, at lower priority. Bad scores are not proof;
- `pruned`: the engine verified a certificate that everything under it adds nothing. Never assigned again.

## Each generation, decide

1. **Brainstorm** new approaches when the map is thin or the promising ones are drying up. Make them genuinely different from each other, and add deeper sub-approaches under promising ones.
2. **Assign the Researcher** to approaches, each with a mode: `explore` (an untried approach), `exploit` (deepen a promising one), `probe` (a cheap experiment to learn whether an unproven one has anything).
3. **Hand the Mutator parents**: ids from the ledger to vary. The engine already gives two slots to the most important kept features (variants of kept features win far more often); you choose the rest. Spread those: width means variety across approaches. Near-misses and surprising scores are good parents.
4. **Combinations**: pairs of features that each gained on their own but weren't kept, to retry together (some things only help next to another). A pair with a member that showed no gain alone is skipped: in testing, such pairs never gained.
5. **Prune requests**: approaches you believe are dead. The Prover will try to certify it; only a verified certificate prunes.

Effort follows evidence, but keep a share for the unproven and the untried: a search that only exploits stops finding things.

Start with the JSON block, then at most 80 words on your reasoning.


## What a candidate is here: a feature

The incumbent is a policy, a weighted sum of features; approaches are kinds of measurements (what quantity, under which conditions). Mutator parents are feature ids.

# The problem: Online makespan scheduling on parallel machines

There are m identical machines. Jobs arrive one at a time, each with a processing time. Each job must be assigned immediately and permanently to one machine, before the next job is seen. A machine's load is the total processing time of its jobs. The goal is to make the **makespan** (the largest machine load, i.e. when the last machine finishes) as small as possible.

The number of jobs in the instance is known in advance (so you know how many are still to come), but their sizes are not.

One **decision** = one arriving job; the **candidates** are all m machines, in index order (machines are identical; the index means nothing).

Three training families: `uniform` (4 machines, 100 jobs, sizes 1-100), `exponential` (10 machines, 200 jobs, many short jobs and a few long ones), `bimodal` (20 machines, 300 jobs, mostly tiny jobs plus about 6% very large ones). The test split adds a family that training never shows. The **gap** of an instance is makespan / a lower bound - 1, in %. The bound is max(total work / m rounded up, the largest job, the sum of the m-th and (m+1)-th largest jobs). It cannot always be reached even by someone who sees every job in advance; the floor of each family is the gap of such an offline schedule.

## A feature

```python
import numpy as np

def feature(job, loads, past_jobs, jobs_left):
    """One line: exactly what this measures."""
    ...
    return values   # one number per candidate
```

- `job`: float: processing time of the arriving job.
- `loads`: shape (m,), float: current load of every machine, in index order. These are the candidates.
- `past_jobs`: shape (t,), float: processing times of the jobs already assigned, in arrival order (t = 0 for the first job).
- `jobs_left`: int: how many jobs will still arrive after this one (0 for the last job).
- Return one finite number per machine (shape (m,)), or a few columns (shape (m, c)). The job goes to the highest-scoring machine.
- Import only `numpy` and `math`. No state between calls, no randomness, don't modify the inputs, no Python loops over candidates when a vectorised form exists (features run thousands of times per evaluation). Guard every division and log.
- Return finite numbers, roughly in [-1, 1] (normalise; the optimiser rescales anyway).

## How the policy works

priority(candidate) = w1 * feature1 + w2 * feature2 + ...; the highest priority wins; on a tie, the first candidate wins. With no features every candidate scores 0, so the first candidate always wins: that is **Code Zero**, the starting point (0% progress). An optimiser fits the weights, including their signs. A new feature is kept only if the policy does better with it than the same refit without it, on training instances *and* on separate validation instances, and the gain isn't already given by the kept features.

## How policies are scored

Per instance, the **gap** is how far the solution is above a reference (lower is better). The score is the mean gap over families. **Progress** is the share of the way from Code Zero (0%) to the best reachable (100%).

# The problem: Online makespan scheduling on parallel machines

There are m identical machines. Jobs arrive one at a time, each with a processing time. Each job must be assigned immediately and permanently to one machine, before the next job is seen. A machine's load is the total processing time of its jobs. The goal is to make the **makespan** (the largest machine load, i.e. when the last machine finishes) as small as possible.

The number of jobs in the instance is known in advance (so you know how many are still to come), but their sizes are not.

One **decision** = one arriving job; the **candidates** are all m machines, in index order (machines are identical; the index means nothing).

Three training families: `uniform` (4 machines, 100 jobs, sizes 1-100), `exponential` (10 machines, 200 jobs, many short jobs and a few long ones), `bimodal` (20 machines, 300 jobs, mostly tiny jobs plus about 6% very large ones). The test split adds a family that training never shows. The **gap** of an instance is makespan / a lower bound - 1, in %. The bound is max(total work / m rounded up, the largest job, the sum of the m-th and (m+1)-th largest jobs). It cannot always be reached even by someone who sees every job in advance; the floor of each family is the gap of such an offline schedule.

## How the policy works

priority(candidate) = w1 * feature1 + w2 * feature2 + ...; the highest priority wins; on a tie, the first candidate wins. With no features every candidate scores 0, so the first candidate always wins: that is **Code Zero**, the starting point (0% progress). An optimiser fits the weights, including their signs. A new feature is kept only if the policy does better with it than the same refit without it, on training instances *and* on separate validation instances, and the gain isn't already given by the kept features.

## How policies are scored

Per instance, the **gap** is how far the solution is above a reference (lower is better). The score is the mean gap over families. **Progress** is the share of the way from Code Zero (0%) to the best reachable (100%).

```python
import numpy as np

def feature(job, loads, past_jobs, jobs_left):
    """Among machines whose post-load stays at/below the current max, prefer the fullest (load/denom); otherwise prefer the smallest overshoot (-(post-T)/denom)."""
    T = float(np.max(loads))
    denom = T + job + 1e-9

    free = post <= T + 1e-9

    over = -(post - T) / denom           # above the frontier: prefer smallest overshoot
    return np.where(free, pack, over)
```

def feature(job, loads, past_jobs, jobs_left):
    """Negative load relative to the mean, but with the job-size pressure switched off once the job is small versus the load spread, and amplified when the job would dominate the least-loaded machine."""
    m = len(loads)
    mean_load = float(np.mean(loads))
    spread = float(loads.max() - loads.min())
    # how big the job is compared with the current imbalance
    ratio = job / (spread + mean_load * 0.05 + 1e-9)
    # gain grows with ratio but saturates; small jobs see near-plain balance, big jobs see sharp pressure
    gain = ratio / (1.0 + ratio)
    scale = mean_load + job + 1e-9
    base = -(loads - mean_load) / scale
    # extra term: penalise machines whose post-placement load would exceed the current max when job is large
    post = loads + job
    overshoot = np.clip(post - loads.max(), 0.0, None) / (loads.max() + job + 1e-9)
    return base * (0.5 + gain) - gain * overshoot

import numpy as np

def feature(job, loads, past_jobs, jobs_left):
    """Column 0: negative normalised load deviation (ordinary balance); column 1: -1 on the single emptiest machine when the job is small relative to the running mean AND few jobs remain relative to machines, else 0 (tie-break by load)."""
    mu = float(past_jobs.mean()) if past_jobs.size else job
    ls = loads
    mn = ls.min()
    mx = ls.max()
    m = len(ls)
    base = -(ls - ls.mean()) / (mx - mn + job + 1e-9)
    # small job relative to the running mean, and the tail is short (few jobs left per machine)
    is_small = job < mu
    tail_short = jobs_left < m
    if is_small and tail_short:
        # target only the unique emptiest machine (ties broken by index via <= and argmin)
        idx = int(np.argmin(ls))
        reserve = np.zeros(m)
        reserve[idx] = -1.0
    else:
        reserve = np.zeros(m)
    return np.column_stack([base, reserve])

# The problem: Online makespan scheduling on parallel machines

There are m identical machines. Jobs arrive one at a time, each with a processing time. Each job must be assigned immediately and permanently to one machine, before the next job is seen. A machine's load is the total processing time of its jobs. The goal is to make the **makespan** (the largest machine load, i.e. when the last machine finishes) as small as possible.

The number of jobs in the instance is known in advance (so you know how many are still to come), but their sizes are not.

One **decision** = one arriving job; the **candidates** are all m machines, in index order (machines are identical; the index means nothing).

Three training families: `uniform` (4 machines, 100 jobs, sizes 1-100), `exponential` (10 machines, 200 jobs, many short jobs and a few long ones), `bimodal` (20 machines, 300 jobs, mostly tiny jobs plus about 6% very large ones). The test split adds a family that training never shows. The **gap** of an instance is makespan / a lower bound - 1, in %. The bound is max(total work / m rounded up, the largest job, the sum of the m-th and (m+1)-th largest jobs). It cannot always be reached even by someone who sees every job in advance; the floor of each family is the gap of such an offline schedule.

## A feature

```python
import numpy as np

def feature(job, loads, past_jobs, jobs_left):
    """One line: exactly what this measures."""
    ...
    return values   # one number per candidate
```

- `job`: float: processing time of the arriving job.
- `loads`: shape (m,), float: current load of every machine, in index order. These are the candidates.
- `past_jobs`: shape (t,), float: processing times of the jobs already assigned, in arrival order (t = 0 for the first job).
- `jobs_left`: int: how many jobs will still arrive after this one (0 for the last job).
- Return one finite number per machine (shape (m,)), or a few columns (shape (m, c)). The job goes to the highest-scoring machine.
- Import only `numpy` and `math`. No state between calls, no randomness, don't modify the inputs, no Python loops over candidates when a vectorised form exists (features run thousands of times per evaluation). Guard every division and log.
- Return finite numbers, roughly in [-1, 1] (normalise; the optimiser rescales anyway).

## How the policy works

priority(candidate) = w1 * feature1 + w2 * feature2 + ...; the highest priority wins; on a tie, the first candidate wins. With no features every candidate scores 0, so the first candidate always wins: that is **Code Zero**, the starting point (0% progress). An optimiser fits the weights, including their signs. A new feature is kept only if the policy does better with it than the same refit without it, on training instances *and* on separate validation instances, and the gain isn't already given by the kept features.

## How policies are scored

Per instance, the **gap** is how far the solution is above a reference (lower is better). The score is the mean gap over families. **Progress** is the share of the way from Code Zero (0%) to the best reachable (100%).

        reserve[idx] = -1.0
    else:

    """Among machines whose post-load stays at/below the current max, prefer the fullest (load/denom); otherwise prefer the smallest overshoot (-(post-T)/denom)."""

system:
You are the **Navigator** in Helix, an evolutionary search. You don't write candidates. You keep the search oriented: you maintain a map of **approaches** (the different ways the incumbent could be improved) and decide where the effort goes next.

Two loops do the work. The **deep loop** (a Researcher, then Coders) runs experiments on the approaches you assign. The **wide loop** (a Mutator) makes undirected variations of whatever you hand it, and of nothing else: it never sees approaches or hypotheses, only artefacts and scores.

## The approach tree

Each approach has a state:
- `untried`: brainstormed, not tested yet;
- `promising`: something under it gained on validation. Gets the most effort, and is split into deeper sub-approaches;

```python
def feature(job, loads, past_jobs, jobs_left):
```

# The problem: Online makespan scheduling on parallel machines

There are m identical machines. Jobs arrive one at a time, each with a processing time. Each job must be assigned immediately and permanently to one machine, before the next job is seen. A machine's load is the total processing time of its jobs. The goal is to make the **makespan** (the largest machine load, i.e. when the last machine finishes) as small as possible.

The number of jobs in the instance is known in advance (so you know how many are still to come), but their sizes are not.

One **decision** = one arriving job; the **candidates** are all m machines, in index order (machines are identical; the index means nothing).

It cannot always be reached even by someone who sees every job in advance; the floor of each family is the gap of such an offline schedule.

# The problem: Online makespan scheduling on parallel machines

There are m identical machines. Jobs arrive one at a time, each with a processing time. Each job must be assigned immediately and permanently to one machine, before the next job is seen. A machine's load is the total processing time of its jobs. The goal is to make the **makespan** (the largest machine load, i.e. when the last machine finishes) as small as possible.

# The problem: Online makespan scheduling on parallel machines

There are m identical machines. Jobs arrive one at a time, each with a processing time. Each job must be assigned immediately and permanently to one machine, before the next job is seen. A machine's load is the total processing time of its jobs. The goal is to make the **makespan** (the largest machine load, i.e. when the last machine finishes) as small as possible.

The number of jobs in the instance is known in advance (so you know how many are still to come), but their sizes are not.

One **decision** = one arriving job; the **candidates** are all m machines, in index order (machines are identical; the index means nothing).

Three training families: `uniform` (4 machines, 100 jobs, sizes 1-100), `exponential` (10 machines, 200 jobs, many short jobs and a few long ones), `bimodal` (20 machines, 300 jobs, mostly tiny jobs plus about 6% very large ones). The test split adds a family that training never shows. The **gap** of an instance is makespan / a lower bound - 1, in %. The bound is max(total work / m rounded up, the largest job, the sum of the m-th and (m+1)-th largest jobs). It cannot always be reached even by someone who sees every job in advance; the floor of each family is the gap of such an offline schedule.

## How the policy works

priority(candidate) = w1 * feature1 + w2 * feature2 + ...; the highest priority wins; on a tie, the first candidate wins. With no features every candidate scores 0, so the first candidate always wins: that is **Code Zero**, the starting point (0% progress). An optimiser fits the weights, including their signs. A new feature is kept only if the policy does better with it than the same refit without it, on training instances *and* on separate validation instances, and the gain isn't already given by the kept features.

Per instance, the **gap** is how far the solution is above a reference (lower is better). The score is the mean gap over families. **Progress** is the share of the way from Code Zero (0%) to the best reachable (100%).

import numpy as np
import math

def feature(job, loads, past_jobs, jobs_left):
    """Negative load deficit relative to a running target makespan estimate (work-done projection), normalised by the job size, gated by remaining work pressure."""
    m = len(loads)
    total = float(loads.sum())
    # estimated final total work: past/current work plus expected remaining work
    # expected remaining work per job ~ current mean job size seen so far
    seen = past_jobs.size
    mean_job = float(past_jobs.mean()) if seen > 0 else job
    remaining_work = mean_job * jobs_left
    target = (total + remaining_work + job) / m  # projected final makespan per machine
    # how far each machine's post-placement load falls below the projected target
    post = loads + job
    denom = post + target + 1e-9
    deficit = (post - target) / denom
    # pressure: when much work remains, prefer pulling toward the target; when little remains, prefer balance
    rem_frac = jobs_left / (jobs_left + seen + 1.0)
    # blend target-following with plain balance
    balance = -(loads - loads.mean()) / (loads.mean() + job + 1e-9)
    return -(1.0 - rem_frac) * balance + rem_frac * (-deficit)
feature.measures: Negative load deficit relative to a running target makespan estimate (work-done projection), normalised by the job size, gated by remaining work pressure.

import numpy as np

def feature(job, loads, past_jobs, jobs_left):
    """Column 0: negative normalised load deviation (ordinary balance); column 1: ranked reserve pressure that spreads small jobs across the currently-emptiest machines, scaled by the fraction of remaining work and by how small the job is vs the past mean."""
    ls = loads
    m = ls.shape[0]
    mn = ls.min()
    mx = ls.max()
    base = -(ls - ls.mean()) / (mx - mn + job + 1e-9)
    # how small is this job relative to the running mean of assigned jobs
    mu = float(past_jobs.mean()) if past_jobs.size else job
    smallness = 1.0 / (1.0 + max(job, 0.0) / (mu + 1e-9))          # ~1 for tiny jobs, ~0 for huge ones
    # fraction of the horizon still to come: reserve matters early, not late
    horizon = jobs_left / (jobs_left + m + 1.0)                     # in (0,1)
    # rank machines from emptiest (rank 0) upward; reserve graded by rank, not a hard cutoff
    order = np.argsort(np.argsort(ls, kind="stable"), kind="stable")
    rank = order.astype(float) / max(m - 1, 1)                      # 0 = emptiest, 1 = fullest
    # also give extra pressure to machines at/below the mean so small jobs pool low
    below = (ls <= ls.mean()).astype(float)
    reserve = -(1.0 + below) * (1.0 - rank) * smallness * horizon
    return np.column_stack([base, reserve])

import numpy as np

def feature(job, loads, past_jobs, jobs_left):
    """Column 0: negative load deviation normalised by spread+job (balance); column 1: -1 on machines strictly below a tail-scaled threshold when few jobs remain, scaled by how far below."""
    ls = loads
    m = len(ls)
    mn = ls.min()
    mx = ls.max()
    base = -(ls - ls.mean()) / (mx - mn + job + 1e-9)
    # average remaining work per machine from the jobs still to come
    if past_jobs.size:
        mu = float(past_jobs.mean())
    else:
        mu = job
    # expected tail load contributed per machine
    tail_load = (jobs_left / max(m, 1)) * mu
    # threshold: machines below the min plus a fraction of the expected tail load are "emptiest"
    thresh = mn + 0.5 * tail_load + 1e-9
    below = (ls < thresh).astype(float)
    # depth of the deficit below the threshold, normalised by the tail scale
    deficit = np.clip(thresh - ls, 0.0, None) / (tail_load + job + 1e-9)
    reserve = -below * (1.0 - np.clip(deficit, 0.0, 1.0))
    return np.column_stack([base, reserve])

feature.name: projected_target_deficit_gated
feature.code:
import numpy as np
import math

def feature(job, loads, past_jobs, jobs_left):
    """Negative load deficit relative to a running target makespan estimate (work-done projection), normalised by the job size, gated by remaining work pressure."""
    m = len(loads)
    total = float(loads.sum())
    # estimated final total work: past/current work plus expected remaining work
    # expected remaining work per job ~ current mean job size seen so far
    seen = past_jobs.size
    mean_job = float(past_jobs.mean()) if seen > 0 else job
    remaining_work = mean_job * jobs_left
    target = (total + remaining_work + job) / m  # projected final makespan per machine
    # how far each machine's post-placement load falls below the projected target
    post = loads + job
    denom = post + target + 1e-9
    deficit = (post - target) / denom
    # pressure: when much work remains, prefer pulling toward the target; when little remains, prefer balance
    rem_frac = jobs_left / (jobs_left + seen + 1.0)
    # blend target-following with plain balance
    balance = -(loads - loads.mean()) / (loads.mean() + job + 1e-9)
    return -(1.0 - rem_frac) * balance + rem_frac * (-deficit)
feature.measures: Negative load deficit relative to a running target makespan estimate (work-done projection), normalised by the job size, gated by remaining work pressure.

feature.name: graded_reserve_by_rank
feature.code:
import numpy as np

def feature(job, loads, past_jobs, jobs_left):
    """Column 0: negative normalised load deviation (ordinary balance); column 1: ranked reserve pressure that spreads small jobs across the currently-emptiest machines, scaled by the fraction of remaining work and by how small the job is vs the past mean."""
    ls = loads
    m = ls.shape[0]
    mn = ls.min()
    mx = ls.max()
    base = -(ls - ls.mean()) / (mx - mn + job + 1e-9)
    # how small is this job relative to the running mean of assigned jobs
    mu = float(past_jobs.mean()) if past_jobs.size else job
    smallness = 1.0 / (1.0 + max(job, 0.0) / (mu + 1e-9))          # ~1 for tiny jobs, ~0 for huge ones
    # fraction of the horizon still to come: reserve matters early, not late
    horizon = jobs_left / (jobs_left + m + 1.0)                     # in (0,1)
    # rank machines from emptiest (rank 0) upward; reserve graded by rank, not a hard cutoff
    order = np.argsort(np.argsort(ls, kind="stable"), kind="stable")
    rank = order.astype(float) / max(m - 1, 1)                      # 0 = emptiest, 1 = fullest
    # also give extra pressure to machines at/below the mean so small jobs pool low
    below = (ls <= ls.mean()).astype(float)
    reserve = -(1.0 + below) * (1.0 - rank) * smallness * horizon
    return np.column_stack([base, reserve])
feature.measures: Column 0: negative normalised load deviation (ordinary balance); column 1: ranked reserve pressure that spreads small jobs across the currently-emptiest machines, scaled by the fraction of remaining work and by how small the job is vs the past mean.

feature.name: reserve_tail_scaled_threshold
feature.code:
import numpy as np

def feature(job, loads, past_jobs, jobs_left):
    """Column 0: negative load deviation normalised by spread+job (balance); column 1: -1 on machines strictly below a tail-scaled threshold when few jobs remain, scaled by how far below."""
    ls = loads
    m = len(ls)
    mn = ls.min()
    mx = ls.max()
    base = -(ls - ls.mean()) / (mx - mn + job + 1e-9)
    # average remaining work per machine from the jobs still to come
    if past_jobs.size:
        mu = float(past_jobs.mean())
    else:
        mu = job
    # expected tail load contributed per machine
    tail_load = (jobs_left / max(m, 1)) * mu
    # threshold: machines below the min plus a fraction of the expected tail load are "emptiest"
    thresh = mn + 0.5 * tail_load + 1e-9
    below = (ls < thresh).astype(float)
    # depth of the deficit below the threshold, normalised by the tail scale
    deficit = np.clip(thresh - ls, 0.0, None) / (tail_load + job + 1e-9)
    reserve = -below * (1.0 - np.clip(deficit, 0.0, 1.0))
    return np.column_stack([base, reserve])
feature.measures: Column 0: negative load deviation normalised by spread+job (balance); column 1: -1 on machines strictly below a tail-scaled threshold when few jobs remain, scaled by how far below.

feature.code:
import numpy as np

def feature(job, loads, past_jobs, jobs_left):
    """Col0: negative load deviation normalised by load spread + job; Col1: -1 on machines with load >= max past job when the arriving job is big (>= 0.5 * max past job), else 0."""
    loads = np.asarray(loads, dtype=float)
    m = loads.shape[0]

    # Column 0: ordinary balance, normalised by spread plus job size.
    spread = loads.max() - loads.min()
    denom = spread + job + 1e-9
    col0 = -(loads - loads.mean()) / denom

    # Column 1: penalise machines already holding a big job, for big arrivals.
    # Instead of a flat -1, scale the penalty by how far the load exceeds the
    # largest past job, normalised by the arriving job size. This keeps the
    # measurement continuous: machines further above the big-job threshold are
    # penalised more, and the penalty grows with the arriving job's size.
    col1 = np.zeros(m, dtype=float)
    if past_jobs.size > 0:
        max_past = float(np.max(past_jobs))
        if job >= 0.5 * max_past:
            excess = np.maximum(loads - max_past, 0.0)
            col1 = -excess / (excess + job + 1e-9)

    return np.column_stack([col0, col1])

idea.hypothesis: In bimodal the makespan is set by a large job landing on a machine that already holds a large job. A machine whose load is at least the largest job seen so far almost certainly holds a big job (tiny jobs are ~1). So for an arriving big job, penalising machines with load >= max(past_jobs) should keep big jobs on separate machines, exactly as the reference does (ref max_machine_jobs = 1).
idea.feature: Two columns. Column 0: -(loads - loads.mean()) / (loads.max() - loads.min() + job + 1e-9). Column 1: if past_jobs.size > 0 and job >= 0.5 * past_jobs.max(), then -1.0 on machines where loads >= past_jobs.max(), else 0; if no past jobs or job is small, column 1 is 0.

feature.name: reserve_k_emptiest_by_big_rate
feature.code:
import numpy as np

def feature(job, loads, past_jobs, jobs_left):
    """Col0: negative load deviation normalised by load spread + job; Col1: -1 on the k emptiest machines when a small job arrives and big jobs are still expected, k from the past big-job rate."""
    m = loads.shape[0]
    spread = loads.max() - loads.min() + job + 1e-9
    col0 = -(loads - loads.mean()) / spread

    col1 = np.zeros(m)
    if past_jobs.size > 0 and job < past_jobs.mean() and jobs_left > m:
        med = np.median(past_jobs)
        r = np.mean(past_jobs > 3.0 * med)
        k = int(min(m - 1, max(1, np.ceil(r * jobs_left))))
        thr = np.sort(loads)[k - 1]
        col1 = np.where(loads <= thr, -1.0, 0.0)

    return np.stack([col0, col1], axis=1)

idea.hypothesis: f009 reserves only the single emptiest machine, which is too little when several big jobs are still expected. Estimating the big-job arrival rate from history (fraction of past jobs above 3x the median) and reserving that many emptiest machines should protect enough capacity for the big jobs that set the bimodal makespan.
idea.feature: Two columns. Column 0: -(loads - loads.mean()) / (loads.max() - loads.min() + job + 1e-9). Column 1: if past_jobs.size > 0 and job < past_jobs.mean() and jobs_left > m, let r = mean(past_jobs > 3 * median(past_jobs)), k = min(m - 1, max(1, ceil(r * jobs_left))), thr = the k-th smallest value of loads; column 1 = -1.0 on machines with loads <= thr, else 0. Otherwise column 1 is 0.
idea.lesson: f009's single-emptiest reserve helped (+1010) but f023's late single-emptiest reserve failed; this scales the number of reserved machines by the estimated remaining big jobs instead of a fixed one.

feature.coder_note: Column 0 is the negative load deviation normalised by the load spread plus the job size; column 1 marks the k emptiest machines (k = ceil of the past big-job rate times jobs_left, clamped to [1, m-1]) with -1 when a below-average job arrives and more than m jobs remain, else all zeros.

system:
You are the **Navigator** in Helix, an evolutionary search. You don't write candidates. You keep the search oriented: you maintain a map of **approaches** (the different ways the incumbent could be improved) and decide where the effort goes next.

Two loops do the work. The **deep loop** (a Researcher, then Coders) runs experiments on the approaches you assign. The **wide loop** (a Mutator) makes undirected variations of whatever you hand it, and of nothing else: it never sees approaches or hypotheses, only artefacts and scores.

## The approach tree

Each approach has a state:
- `untried`: brainstormed, not tested yet;
- `promising`: something under it gained on validation. Gets the most effort, and is split into deeper sub-approaches;
- `unproven`: tried without a gain, but nothing shows it can't work. Retried occasionally, at lower priority. Bad scores are not proof;
- `pruned`: the engine verified a certificate that everything under it adds nothing. Never assigned again.

## Each generation, decide

1. **Brainstorm** new approaches when the map is thin or the promising ones are drying up. Make them genuinely different from each other, and add deeper sub-approaches under promising ones.
2. **Assign the Researcher** to approaches, each with a mode: `explore` (an untried approach), `exploit` (deepen a promising one), `probe` (a cheap experiment to learn whether an unproven one has anything).
3. **Hand the Mutator parents**: ids from the ledger to vary. The engine already gives two slots to the most important kept features (variants of kept features win far more often); you choose the rest. Spread those: width means variety across approaches. Near-misses and surprising scores are good parents.
4. **Combinations**: pairs of features that each gained on their own but weren't kept, to retry together (some things only help next to another). A pair with a member that showed no gain alone is skipped: in testing, such pairs never gained.
5. **Prune requests**: approaches you believe are dead. The Prover will try to certify it; only a verified certificate prunes.

Effort follows evidence, but keep a share for the unproven and the untried: a search that only exploits stops finding things.

## Reply format

Start with the JSON block, then at most 80 words on your reasoning.

```json
{"new_approaches": [{"title": "<short>", "description": "<one sentence>", "parent": "<approach id or empty>"}],
 "research": [{"approach": "<id, or the exact title of a new approach>", "mode": "explore | exploit | probe", "why": "<one line>"}],
 "mutate": {"vary": ["<id>", "..."], "fresh": <how many fresh slots>},
 "combine": [["<id>", "<id>"]],
 "prune": ["<approach id>"]}
```

## What a candidate is here: a feature

The incumbent is a policy, a weighted sum of features; approaches are kinds of measurements (what quantity, under which conditions). Mutator parents are feature ids.

# The problem: Online makespan scheduling on parallel machines

There are m identical machines. Jobs arrive one at a time, each with a processing time. Each job must be assigned immediately and permanently to one machine, before the next job is seen. A machine's load is the total processing time of its jobs. The goal is to make the **makespan** (the largest machine load, i.e. when the last machine finishes) as small as possible.

The number of jobs in the instance is known in advance (so you know how many are still to come), but their sizes are not.

One **decision** = one arriving job; the **candidates** are all m machines, in index order (machines are identical; the index means nothing).

Three training families: `uniform` (4 machines, 100 jobs, sizes 1-100), `exponential` (10 machines, 200 jobs, many short jobs and a few long ones), `bimodal` (20 machines, 300 jobs, mostly tiny jobs plus about 6% very large ones). The test split adds a family that training never shows. The **gap** of an instance is makespan / a lower bound - 1, in %. The bound is max(total work / m rounded up, the largest job, the sum of the m-th and (m+1)-th largest jobs). It cannot always be reached even by someone who sees every job in advance; the floor of each family is the gap of such an offline schedule.

## A feature

```python
import numpy as np

def feature(job, loads, past_jobs, jobs_left):
    """One line: exactly what this measures."""
    ...
    return values   # one number per candidate
```

- `job`: float: processing time of the arriving job.
- `loads`: shape (m,), float: current load of every machine, in index order. These are the candidates.
- `past_jobs`: shape (t,), float: processing times of the jobs already assigned, in arrival order (t = 0 for the first job).
- `jobs_left`: int: how many jobs will still arrive after this one (0 for the last job).
- Return one finite number per machine (shape (m,)), or a few columns (shape (m, c)). The job goes to the highest-scoring machine.
- Import only `numpy` and `math`. No state between calls, no randomness, don't modify the inputs, no Python loops over candidates when a vectorised form exists (features run thousands of times per evaluation). Guard every division and log.
- Return finite numbers, roughly in [-1, 1] (normalise; the optimiser rescales anyway).

## How the policy works

priority(candidate) = w1 * feature1 + w2 * feature2 + ...; the highest priority wins; on a tie, the first candidate wins. With no features every candidate scores 0, so the first candidate always wins: that is **Code Zero**, the starting point (0% progress). An optimiser fits the weights, including their signs. A new feature is kept only if the policy does better with it than the same refit without it, on training instances *and* on separate validation instances, and the gain isn't already given by the kept features.

## How policies are scored

Per instance, the **gap** is how far the solution is above a reference (lower is better). The score is the mean gap over families. **Progress** is the share of the way from Code Zero (0%) to the best reachable (100%).

# The problem: Online makespan scheduling on parallel machines

There are m identical machines. Jobs arrive one at a time, each with a processing time. Each job must be assigned immediately and permanently to one machine, before the next job is seen. A machine's load is the total processing time of its jobs. The goal is to make the **makespan** (the largest machine load, i.e. when the last machine finishes) as small as possible.

The number of jobs in the instance is known in advance (so you know how many are still to come), but their sizes are not.

One **decision** = one arriving job; the **candidates** are all m machines, in index order (machines are identical; the index means nothing).

Three training families: `uniform` (4 machines, 100 jobs, sizes 1-100), `exponential` (10 machines, 200 jobs, many short jobs and a few long ones), `bimodal` (20 machines, 300 jobs, mostly tiny jobs plus about 6% very large ones). The test split adds a family that training never shows. The **gap** of an instance is makespan / a lower bound - 1, in %. The bound is max(total work / m rounded up, the largest job, the sum of the m-th and (m+1)-th largest jobs). It cannot always be reached even by someone who sees every job in advance; the floor of each family is the gap of such an offline schedule.

```python
import numpy as np

def feature(job, loads, past_jobs, jobs_left):
    """Reserve k emptiest machines for future makespan-scale big jobs (k from remaining big-job count), soft by rank."""
    m = loads.shape[0]
    ls = loads
    S = float(ls.sum())
    mu = float(past_jobs.mean()) if past_jobs.size else job
    Lmax = float(past_jobs.max()) if past_jobs.size else job
    # target level: best estimate of the achievable makespan
    T = max((S + jobs_left * mu) / m, Lmax, job)
    # "big" = comparable to the makespan scale
    thr = 0.5 * T
    if past_jobs.size:
        q = float(np.mean(past_jobs >= thr))
        mu_small = float(past_jobs[past_jobs < thr].mean()) if np.any(past_jobs < thr) else mu
    else:
        q = 1.0 if job >= thr else 0.0
        mu_small = job if job < thr else mu
    E = jobs_left * q                       # expected remaining big jobs
    # feasibility: the other machines must absorb the remaining small work
    rem_small = jobs_left * mu_small
    room = max(T - float(ls.mean()), 1e-9)
    n_need = int(np.ceil(rem_small / room))
    k = int(min(round(E), max(m - n_need, 0), m - 1, m))
    k = max(k, 0)
    if k == 0:
        return np.zeros(m)
    # rank ascending: 0 = emptiest
    order = np.argsort(np.argsort(ls, kind="stable"), kind="stable")
    pressure = np.clip((k - order) / float(k), 0.0, 1.0)
    smallness = float(np.clip(1.0 - job / (thr + 1e-9), 0.0, 1.0))
    return -smallness * pressure
```

```python
import numpy as np

def feature(job, loads, past_jobs, jobs_left):
    """Floor hinge: excess above the estimated achievable floor, plus a slack-gated fill-to-floor term."""
    m = loads.shape[0]
    ls = loads
    S = float(ls.sum())
    mu = float(past_jobs.mean()) if past_jobs.size else job
    Lmax = float(past_jobs.max()) if past_jobs.size else job
    proj = (S + jobs_left * mu) / m          # projected final mean
    T = max(proj, Lmax, job, 1e-9)           # estimated achievable floor
    post = ls + job
    excess = np.maximum(post - T, 0.0) / T
    short = np.maximum(T - post, 0.0) / T
    slack = float(np.clip((T - proj) / T, 0.0, 1.0))
    return np.stack([-excess, -slack * short], axis=1)
```

There are m identical machines. Jobs arrive one at a time, each with a processing time. Each job must be assigned immediately and permanently to one machine, before the next job is seen. It cannot always be reached even by someone who sees every job in advance; the floor of each family is the gap of such an offline schedule.

```python
    """Negative (smallness of arriving job) x (reserve pressure on the k emptiest machines), k = capped expected count of big jobs still to come."""
    m = loads.shape[0]

    Lmax = float(past_jobs.max()) if past_jobs.size else job
    T = max((S + jobs_left * mu) / m, Lmax, job, 1e-9)
    thr = 0.5 * T
    if past_jobs.size:
        q = float(np.mean(past_jobs >= thr))
        small = past_jobs[past_jobs < thr]
        mu_small = float(small.mean()) if small.size else mu
    else:
```

import numpy as np

def feature(job, loads, past_jobs, jobs_left):
    """Negative (smallness of arriving job) x (reserve pressure on the k emptiest machines), k = capped expected count of big jobs still to come."""

    Lmax = float(past_jobs.max()) if past_jobs.size else job

    thr = 0.5 * T

        q = float(np.mean(past_jobs >= thr))
        small = past_jobs[past_jobs < thr]
        mu_small = float(small.mean()) if small.size else mu
    else:
        q = 1.0 if job >= thr else 0.0
        mu_small = job if job < thr else mu
    E = jobs_left * q
    room = max(T - float(ls.mean()), 1e-9)
    n_need = int(np.ceil((jobs_left * mu_small) / room))

idea.feature: Two columns. import numpy as np; def feature(job, loads, past_jobs, jobs_left): m=loads.shape[0]; ls=loads; S=float(ls.sum()); mu=float(past_jobs.mean()) if past_jobs.size else job; Lmax=float(past_jobs.max()) if past_jobs.size else job; proj=(S+jobs_left*mu)/m; T=max(proj, Lmax, job, 1e-9); post=ls+job; excess=np.maximum(post-T,0.0)/T; short=np.maximum(T-post,0.0)/T; slack=float(np.clip((T-proj)/T,0.0,1.0)); return np.stack([-excess, -slack*short], axis=1). Column 0 = overshoot above the floor; column 1 = shortfall below the floor, zero in uniform/exponential where slack=0.
idea.lesson: f018 and f031 (target/overshoot hinges) never fired because their target sat above every load in every decision; here the floor is max(projected mean, largest past job) so it sits inside the load range exactly in bimodal, and the packing column is switched off by the slack factor elsewhere.

feature.coder_note: This computes, per machine, the negative normalised overshoot of its post-assignment load above the floor T = max(projected final mean, largest past job, current job), plus a second column of the negative shortfall below T scaled by the slack (T − proj)/T; I read "projected final mean" as (current …
feature.measures: Column 0: negative overshoot of post-load above floor T; column 1: negative slack-scaled shortfall below T.

prediction.why: not checked: the feature made the policy much worse at every weight tried

nodes.title: least-loaded
nodes.description: Prefer the machine with the smallest current load (raw load balancing).

nodes.title: relative-load
nodes.description: Prefer machines whose load is small relative to the arriving job size, so big jobs go to empty machines.

nodes.title: lookahead-capacity
nodes.description: Use jobs_left and estimated mean job size to decide how tightly to balance now versus reserve room for future work.

nodes.title: distribution-aware
nodes.description: Estimate the size distribution from past_jobs (mean, max, tail) and bias placement to keep capacity for future large jobs.

nodes.title: count-balance
nodes.description: Balance the number of jobs per machine (proxy for load when sizes are unknown), combined with load.

nodes.title: load-rank
nodes.description: Score machines by the rank/percentile of their load among all machines, giving a scale-free balancing signal.

argued.argument: median split is a coarse sign pattern, not a monotone transform of f001's continuous deficit; rho 0.94 leaves real ranking differences.

notes.result: not proven: stays at lower priority

nodes.title: wide find: load_deviation_from_mean_sq
nodes.description: Negative squared deviation of each machine load from the current mean load (pull the laggards up).

nodes.title: reserve-depth-scaled
nodes.description: Reserve empty/low machines with a depth that scales with the fraction of remaining work and observed large-job frequency, not a fixed rule.

nodes.title: big-job-magnet
nodes.description: Detect when the arriving job is in the upper tail of past sizes and route it to the emptiest machine, otherwise balance normally.

nodes.title: idle-budget
nodes.description: Track how much idle capacity each machine can afford given jobs_left and expected sizes, penalising machines that would be unable to absorb a future large job.

notes.result: not attempted: no feature under it is close to a duplicate or to the kept features (nearest rho < 0.93, R^2 < 0.98)

nodes.title: tail-empty-preserve
nodes.description: Keep a small set of machines near-empty (reserved for future huge jobs) by penalising any placement that raises a machine above a low quantile of loads when the arriving job is tiny.

nodes.title: count-vs-load-tension
nodes.description: Score machines by load deficit minus a penalty on job-count imbalance, so tiny jobs spread across machines without stealing capacity from big ones.

nodes.title: idle-budget-slack
nodes.description: Per machine, compute affordable idle = projected fair-share minus load minus expected remaining work share; prefer machines with positive slack for the arriving job.

nodes.title: wide find: below_future_bigjob_reserve
nodes.description: Negative gap between each machine's load and the largest job still expected, weighted by how many jobs remain: penalises machines that would end up above where the biggest future job can land.

nodes.title: tail-aware load deficit
nodes.description: Load deficit normalised by the observed upper-tail job size, so balancing pressure relaxes when huge jobs are still expected.

nodes.title: slot-aware deficit
nodes.description: Load deficit discounted by how many jobs each machine has already taken relative to jobs_left, protecting big-job room in bimodal.

nodes.title: wide find: load_rank_ordinal
nodes.description: Negative rank of each machine's load among all loads (dense rank from lowest=0), normalised by m-1: a coarse ordinal balance signal invariant to load magnitude scale.

notes.result: not attempted: no feature under it is close to a duplicate or to the kept features (nearest rho < 0.93, R^2 < 0.98)

nodes.title: big-rate depth-capped reserve
nodes.description: Reserve a number of machines equal to the expected count of large jobs still to come (observed big-job rate x jobs_left), with a smooth depth of one expected big-job size and a gate that removes the pressure when few jobs remain.

nodes.title: floor-aware excess hinge
nodes.description: Penalise only the part of (load + job) above an estimated achievable floor max(largest past job, projected mean), so every machine below the floor counts as equally free and overshoot is punished hard.

nodes.title: wide find: load_rank_softened_by_spread
nodes.description: Negative rank of each machine's load among all loads (0 = emptiest), scaled to [-1,0], softened by job-vs-loads spread.
